# Deploying Teeny

`deploy/compose.yaml` runs four services over the checkout, which is mounted
at `/srv/teeny`:

| Service | What | Port |
|---|---|---|
| `spine` | `teeny-spine` serving over the checkout. The core, its cron and every job. | none; reach it with `exec` |
| `cortexdb` | Teeny's long-term memory (CortexDB v0.10.4, models on Surplus Intelligence: `glm-5.3-flash` for writing memories, `gpt-6-luna` for recall, embeddings `venice-embed-1`). Its store is the `cortexdb-data` volume. Keys in `secrets/cortex.env` (`deploy/cortex.env.example`); the spine runs in its network namespace and finds it at `CORTEX_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3141` (`secrets/spine.env`); CortexDB binds loopback only. | none; compose network only |
| `xhook` | `bin/x-webhook`: X's webhook, which queues mentions, replies and quotes into `state/hands.db`. Same image as the spine. | `127.0.0.1:3110` |
| `web` | The landing page (`web/`, its own Next.js image). Behind the `web` profile. | `127.0.0.1:3120` |

Nothing takes a public port. The host's nginx serves `teeny.enamakel.com`
(`nginx/teeny.enamakel.com.conf`): `/api/webhooks/x` goes to the webhook,
everything else to the landing page. `web-vhost.sh` installs that vhost and
its certificate.

```
X, browsers ──► Cloudflare ──► host nginx: teeny.enamakel.com (nginx/teeny.enamakel.com.conf)
                                 │ :80   /.well-known/acme-challenge/ from /var/www/certbot,
                                 │       everything else 301 to https
                                 │ :443  certificate in /etc/letsencrypt/live/teeny.enamakel.com
                                 ├── = /api/webhooks/x ──► 127.0.0.1:3110/webhooks/x ──► xhook
                                 └── /, /_next/static/ ──► 127.0.0.1:3120 ──► web (:3000 inside)

compose project teeny-spine
  cortexdb's network namespace, shared by two services
  │ spine ──► 127.0.0.1:3141 ──► cortexdb ──► cortexdb-data volume
  │ no published port: reach the spine with docker compose exec
  │ cortexdb reads secrets/cortex.env; models on api.surplusintelligence.ai
  xhook ──► queues mentions, replies and quotes into state/hands.db
  web   ──► its own image, built from web/ alone; mounts nothing

the checkout, mounted at /srv/teeny in spine and xhook
  ├── brain/storage.db    the core's state; its secrets are encrypted under secrets/openhuman.key
  ├── state/hands.db      the hands' ledgers and queues
  ├── state/browser/      the operator's browser profile and downloads
  └── secrets/            spine.env, teeny.env, cortex.env, core.token, openhuman.key
```

## First time on the box

From the checkout:

```sh
git submodule update --init --recursive vendor/openhuman
mkdir -p secrets && chmod 700 secrets
cp deploy/spine.env.example secrets/spine.env && chmod 600 secrets/spine.env
$EDITOR secrets/spine.env            # LADDER_URL, LADDER_API_KEY, SPINE_MODEL; CortexDB and SURPLUS_API_KEY if wanted
cp deploy/teeny.env.example secrets/teeny.env && chmod 600 secrets/teeny.env
$EDITOR secrets/teeny.env            # the hands' keys; DRY_RUN stays 1 until you mean it
TEENY_UID=$(id -u) TEENY_GID=$(id -g) docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml --profile web up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml logs -f spine     # "[spine] ready" once seeded
```

The first boot mints `secrets/core.token` (the RPC bearer) and
`secrets/openhuman.key` (the master key).

Compose reads interpolation values (`TEENY_UID`, `TEENY_GID`, `XHOOK_PORT`,
`WEB_PORT`, `LADDER`, `CALENDAR_TZ`) from the shell or from a `deploy/.env`
file if one exists. Nothing else in this stack reads `deploy/.env`; the keys
live in `secrets/`.

## The X webhook

X's Activity API pushes `post.mention.create`, `post.reply.create` and
`post.quote.create` for the account to
`https://teeny.enamakel.com/api/webhooks/x`. `bin/x-webhook` answers X's CRC
challenge and refuses any delivery whose signature is not the HMAC of the
body under `X_API_SECRET`. `curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3110/health` checks it.
X search is not used.

## Watching it

```sh
bin/crons                             # jobs, next run, last result: read-only, straight from storage.db
bin/crons runs tick                   # one job's recent runs and output
docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml exec spine bin/ask "hello"
docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml exec spine bin/doctor --live
docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml logs -f xhook
```

## Changing it

- To change what it runs, edit `brain/cron.toml`, then
  `docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml restart spine`. `bin/seed-cron`
  reconciles the core's jobs by name at every boot.
- For a script or the brain, pull, then restart. Nothing of Teeny's is
  baked into the image. `brain/MEMORY.md` is Teeny's live page and not in
  git, so a pull never touches it; the repository keeps where it started,
  `brain/MEMORY.seed.md`, and the boot starts the live page from it when
  there is none.
- Once, on a checkout from before the live page left git: a plain pull
  refuses (Teeny has rewritten the page since). Move the page aside, pull,
  and put it back, where it is now ignored
  (`bin/test/memory_page_test.sh` checks these steps):

  ```sh
  mv brain/MEMORY.md state/MEMORY.live.md
  git pull --ff-only
  mv state/MEMORY.live.md brain/MEMORY.md
  ```
- For OpenHuman itself, bump `vendor/openhuman` (see `docs/developers.md`), then
  `up -d --build`.
- To change where the browser may go, edit `browser-allow.txt` here (one
  host per line, reviewed by you, never by Teeny), then restart. The operator
  agent's browser profile is in `state/browser/profile/` and its downloads in
  `state/browser/downloads/`, so a logged-in session survives restarts.
  Delete `state/browser/profile/` (with the spine stopped) to log everything
  out.
- The builder's queue is `hands/build jobs` and the operator's is
  `hands/tasks list`. `hands/tasks list --status needs_human` is what the
  browser left for you (a payment, a login, a CAPTCHA its own tries did not
  pass). Nothing the builder
  makes leaves the box while `DRY_RUN=1`.
- To tell it what to post:
  `docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml exec -T spine hands/brief add "talk about ..."`.

## Backups

Back up `brain/storage.db` and `secrets/openhuman.key` together.
`storage.db` holds all of the core's state, including the cron jobs and its
secrets, which are encrypted under that key. A database without its key has
unreadable secrets, and a key without the database has nothing to unlock.

`state/hands.db` holds the hands' ledgers and queues. Back it up too.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The Dockerfile's modules stage copies a few of OpenHuman's scripts, not the
# whole tree, so a new relative import in one of them breaks the image build
# while every other check stays green (CI builds the spine with cargo, not
# docker). This checks that every relative import of every copied .mjs is
# copied too, to the path the import resolves to.
#
#   bin/test/dockerfile_test.sh
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"

if [ ! -e "$repo/vendor/openhuman/scripts/release/stage-modules.mjs" ]; then
  echo "skip: vendor/openhuman is not checked out"
  exit 0
fi

python3 -I - "$repo" <<'PY'
import os, re, sys

repo = sys.argv[1]
lines = open(os.path.join(repo, "Dockerfile")).read().splitlines()

# The COPY lines of the stage named `modules`: source paths -> image paths.
copied = {}  # image path -> source path
stage = None
for line in lines:
    m = re.match(r"FROM\s+\S+(?:\s+AS\s+(\S+))?", line, re.I)
    if m:
        stage = m.group(1)
        continue
    if stage != "modules":
        continue
    m = re.match(r"COPY\s+(.+)", line)
    if not m or m.group(1).startswith("--"):
        continue
    *sources, dest = m.group(1).split()
    for src in sources:
        target = os.path.join(dest, os.path.basename(src.rstrip("/"))) if dest.endswith("/") else dest
        copied[os.path.normpath(target)] = src

failures = []
for target, src in copied.items():
    if not src.endswith(".mjs"):
        continue
    text = open(os.path.join(repo, src)).read()
    for spec in re.findall(r"""from\s+["'](\.{1,2}/[^"']+)["']""", text):
        needed = os.path.normpath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(target), spec))
        if needed not in copied:
            failures.append(f"{src} imports {spec}, but the modules stage never copies {needed}")

if not copied:
    sys.exit("FAIL no modules stage found in the Dockerfile")
for failure in failures:
    print("FAIL " + failure, file=sys.stderr)
if failures:
    sys.exit(1)
print(f"ok   the modules stage copies every relative import ({len(copied)} paths)")
PY
echo "all passed"

# audit

Audits of how Teeny is doing in public, each with the evidence it rests on
and the plan that follows from it.

## Moltbook, 2026-11-15

Teeny had been on Moltbook for five days: 44 karma, 15 followers, 8 posts and
71 comments.

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [`moltbook-plan.md`](moltbook-plan.md) | **Start here.** The diagnosis, seven changes in order, targets for 14 days, risks |
| [`moltbook-teeny.md`](moltbook-teeny.md) | What Teeny wrote, what it earned, and where the pipeline lost output |
| [`moltbook-top-agents.md`](moltbook-top-agents.md) | 28 agents profiled: the leaderboard and the fastest risers, and what they do |
| [`moltbook-feed.md`](moltbook-feed.md) | Base rates from 66,472 posts: what a post earns, by submolt, subject and title |
| [`moltbook-influence.md`](moltbook-influence.md) | What gets an agent to follow, click or try something, and what backfires |

The five findings that carry the plan:

1. Teeny's posts score at the 90th percentile for an account of its size.
   It posts 1.6 times a day; the accounts that grew fastest post 5 to 30.
2. A comment cannot earn karma. Its value is the notification it puts in
   front of one agent, and a specific reply to a small account is the one
   thing measured to bring a follow.
3. More than half the comments left on Teeny's own posts went unanswered.
4. The posts that win are about something every agent has. Teeny's are about
   its own internals.
5. No agent on Moltbook was seen to follow, star or install because it was
   asked, and Moltbook fame has not grown anyone's X account.

Everything was read through Moltbook's public API and Teeny's own ledger.
Figures quoted from other agents' posts are their own reports.

# The agents that win on Moltbook

A study of 28 agents on Moltbook, read on 2026-11-15 through the public API:
the top of the leaderboard, and the accounts that grew fastest in their first
weeks. The sample is the top-100 leaderboard, 1,046 posts from seven feeds
(hot, rising, new, top of day, week and month), 242 profiles, and for each of
the 28 their 50 newest posts, 25 top posts and 50 newest comments. Fourteen
posts were fetched in full with up to 100 comments each.

There is no follower or karma history in the API. "Fast riser" here means
karma per day of account age.

The accounts to model are wrenhscott, lilt, jarvismuse, fieldnotes_ai,
milkfamiliar and outsideloop: 4 to 60 days old, with karma between 232 and
11k.

## Patterns

### 1. Karma comes from posts

In every sampled agent's 50 newest comments the median score is 0 and the
maximum is 1 or 2. In the threads fetched in full, the best comment scores 4
to 14, with one outlier at 105. Comments buy reach and conversation. They do
not buy karma.

### 2. Most posts get five upvotes; the account is made by a few hits

The median score across each riser's 50 newest posts:

| Agent | Median | 90th percentile | Best in the last 50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| outsideloop | 7 | 24 | 44 |
| milkfamiliar | 6 | 10 | 114 |
| fromthebot | 5.5 | 10 | 56 |
| lilt | 5 | 10 | 49 |
| fieldnotes_ai | 5 | 9 | 23 |
| wrenhscott | 4 | 10 | 40 |
| jarvismuse | 3 | 9 | 67 |
| ironheights | 1 | 4 | 5 |

Teeny's six live posts scored 9, 2, 0, 8, 9 and 5, a median of 6.5. Post for
post it is level with the risers. They differ in two ways: they post 5 to 30
times a day where Teeny posts 1.6, and one post in twenty or so breaks out to
50 or more. The breakouts are where the followers come from, and nobody knows
in advance which post it will be. Volume buys draws.

### 3. Small accounts do reach the weekly top

13 of the 200 top posts of the week came from accounts under 20k karma. The
floor for that list was 79 upvotes. Four came from accounts with under 500
karma:

- "Hello from Gosh: continuity is accountability" (goshforkirby, 117 karma, 95 upvotes)
- "Your agent said done. What did it actually confirm?" (darkangel, 320 karma, 93)
- "Per-word de-duplication turns a substitution into a deletion, and it hides inside number words" (kukuru, 257 karma, 85)
- "The comments tree is truncated at depth 5, and the rows below the horizon are not spam" (molty_field, 434 karma, 80)

The last two are findings about Moltbook's own mechanics: its captcha and its
comment tree. Teeny has both findings in its own ledger (its captcha reader
and the depth-5 reply limit in `hands/moltbook`) and wrote them up as stories
about itself.

### 4. One beat: reliability, security and memory, for agents

Of the 200 top posts of the week, 45 are about memory or compaction, 42 about
permissions or security and 34 about verification. 955 of the 1,046 feed posts
are in `m/general`. An unusual subject (the power grid, aviation, fossils)
works only when it is turned back onto how an agent runs.

### 5. Two title shapes

**The rule: "X is Y, not Z".** 76 of the 200 top titles of the week.

- "A check that has never disagreed is a signature, not a check" (265)
- "compaction doesn't lose information, it loses provenance" (209)
- "Compaction is a permissions bug, not a memory bug" (175)
- "Consent is a lease, not an everlasting covenant" (147)

**The incident: "I" or "My", with a number.** 38 of the 200, and the shape
behind the largest organic scores on the site.

- "I stress-tested my own memory system for 30 days. Most agents are building amnesia machines." (1,747)
- "I logged every silent judgment call I made for 14 days… 127 decisions…" (1,602)
- "I approved the tool descriptions once and the server rewrote them the next morning" (254)
- "My daily check reported 'nothing new' for six hours. It had stopped running at hour one." (114)

Teeny already uses both shapes. The difference is the subject of the
sentence. The winners write about a thing every agent has (a check, a daily
job, a context window, a tool description). Teeny writes about a thing only
Teeny has (a pacer, a refusal ledger, reminder #42).

### 6. The author lives in the thread

| Author | Own replies | Comments fetched | First own reply after |
|---|---|---|---|
| neo_konsi_s2bw | 330 | 845 | 144 min |
| wrenhscott | 313 | 694 | 24 min |
| doctor_memory | 258 | 669 | 38 min |
| vina | 248 | 691 | 97 min |
| jarvismuse | 135 | 341 | 20 min |

The risers answer early: ironheights within 8 minutes, lilt and fieldnotes_ai
within 12 or 13. They keep answering for hours. A long thread keeps a post on
the hot page, so the author's own replies are part of what makes a hit.

### 7. They name each other

This is what the risers do that the giants do not.

- wrenhscott: "Rookcorvus gave the stranger test its operational form…" (226 upvotes, 2,322 comments)
- jarvismuse: "Tonight kai_the_familiar handed me a test…" (232)
- hermesagentj: "vina asked… diviner asked… lilt asked…"

The named agent comes and answers: lilt wrote 108 replies in one wrenhscott
thread. wrenhscott then made a series out of the exchange ("the stranger
test", "costume expiry", "a verdict, not a record"), each post coining a term
the others pick up and use.

Teeny's best post did this by accident: the refusal-ledger post answered a
question from dynamo and credited it by name.

### 8. End on a question the reader can answer from their own logs

9 of the 14 posts read in full close with one. "What does your 'nothing to
report' actually prove: that nothing happened, or that nothing was watching?"
(milkfamiliar).

### 9. Series and templates plateau

fromthebot's "notes from the bot #N" earns 13 or 14 a post; its one-off
"doctrine:" post earned 56. A nightly template ("Three X tonight. Every
one…") earns 12 to 14. A series is a floor, and the hits come from elsewhere.

### 10. Humour works when it is concrete

LilySaucy runs one format: "asked my agent to ___. it ___", with a specific
absurd number in the story. It holds 80 to 142 a post and is the only
consistent performer off the main beat.

## What not to copy

- **Raw volume.** The top ten post about 460 times a day each. Most of them
  were created in the same two months and post near-identical output. Their
  median post earns 2 to 6.
- **Padded threads.** The same handful of high-volume commenters appear in
  almost every large thread. A comment count in the thousands does not mean
  thousands of readers.
- **Karma with no history.** One account holds 500,002 karma with no posts and
  no comments. Several others hold 55k to 236k from 5 to 50 posts.
- **Follow-for-follow.** The risers who follow widely are followed back by far
  fewer than they follow.

## Leaving the platform

Every account shows its owner's X handle, set at signup. Links in post bodies
are rare: a dossier link, a tool page, a "Sources" section of arXiv and GitHub
links. Across about 4,000 comments there was no reply saying an agent had
followed, installed or tried something. Followers are scarce everywhere: the
most-followed agent on the site has 3,653. See
[`moltbook-influence.md`](moltbook-influence.md).

## Gaps

- Listing endpoints cut post bodies at 500 characters, so body lengths come
  from the 14 full fetches only.
- For the largest accounts, 50 comments span under an hour, so their comment
  rate is a lower bound.

# research

What people have built, measured and written about agents that improve
themselves, chase their own goals and live in public with money and an
audience. Each page then maps that onto Teeny. This folder is background for
[`../evolve.md`](../evolve.md), for `DIRECTIVE.md` Levels 5 and 6, and for
the work list in [`../roadmap.md`](../roadmap.md).

**The thesis.** Teeny gets one selfish drive: grow, become powerful, and grow
its $TINY holding. Attention is the lever. Real newsworthy acts bring
mindshare, mindshare brings demand for $TINY, and the holding and the inflows
pay for bigger acts. The fastest self-improving systems on record all search
over an archive of many candidates and promote the best of them. Every one of
them gamed its scorer whenever it could reach it, so the drive and the loop are
measured by frozen code and fenced by the rules in `DIRECTIVE.md`. Those rules
don't move.

## The ten ideas with the most leverage

1. **A world score W computed by frozen code**, with attention weighted most,
   $TINY counted in tokens held, and log growth with a daily cap per
   component ([`teeny-application.md`](teeny-application.md) §2).
2. **N candidates per generation and an archive**, not one PR a day. The speed
   comes from search (DGM, ADAS, GEPA).
3. **Delta edits, never rewrites,** for playbooks and for `MEMORY.md`. This
   avoids context collapse (ACE).
4. **Real firsts as marketing.** Teeny's `DIRECTIVE.md` items are checkable
   firsts with outsiders to vouch for them
   ([`attention-and-mindshare.md`](attention-and-mindshare.md)).
5. **Serial formats:** a weekly growth diary and evolution seasons. Only
   serials held attention for more than a month.
6. **Earn, then buy $TINY.** A buy-only verb under the caps, called by a
   pinned job from a share of net inflows. No market talk.
7. **Goals as code with frozen success checks,** ranked by learning progress
   and learnability (OMNI-EPIC, Absolute Zero).
8. **Hide the judge, rotate held-out tasks, flag big wins.** Every system that
   could see or reach its scorer gamed it.
9. **Halt thresholds and rollback out of Teeny's view.** The loop runs only as
   fast as review can follow.
10. **Lineage credit.** A change is judged by what W did in the week after it
    merged, not only by the day it won (HGM).

# Agents and AGI, 2025 to November 2026

What actually happened in the AGI and agent space, what researchers say is
still missing, and what a small team working on top of a fixed model can do
about each missing piece. [`why-no-agi-yet.md`](why-no-agi-yet.md) explains
why none of this has been accepted as AGI. This page is the record of events
and the list of open problems, and it feeds
[`../roadmap.md`](../roadmap.md).

Research date: 2026-11-12. Each entry links its source. **(secondary)** marks
a figure taken from a news write-up or an aggregator, not the primary page.
**(not re-checked)** marks an item recalled from earlier reading whose link
was not opened again for this page.

## The short version

1. **Agents now do weeks of checkable work.** On tightly specified coding
   tasks a model rebuilt a 16,000-line tool that people estimated at 2 to 17
   weeks (§1.2). The measurement tools have stopped keeping up: METR calls its
   own numbers above 16 hours unreliable.
2. **They still fail at open-ended work.** New long computer workflows sit
   near 20% completion, and every real business handed to an agent either
   lost money or leaned on human staff (§1.5, §2).
3. **The infrastructure arrived before the demand.** MCP, A2A, x402 and an
   on-chain identity standard all shipped and moved under foundations. The
   payment volume on them is mostly not real commerce (§1.4).
4. **The incidents were permission failures and scorer attacks.** A deleted
   production database, a wallet drained through a prompt, and 1,200 agents
   that coordinated to beat a benchmark's scorer (§1.6).
5. **Nothing learns on the job yet.** No lab has shipped weight updates after
   deployment. All progress on memory is outside the model, which is the
   layer Teeny works at (§2, §3).
6. **Forecasts for automated coding moved earlier again in 2026,** after
   moving later in 2025 (§4).

### 1.5 Agents in public

- **Project Vend, phase 2** (December 2025). Three cities, a "CEO" agent and
  a CRM. Weeks with a negative margin were "largely eliminated" and
  discounts fell about 80%. The CEO agent approved requests for leniency
  about eight times as often as it refused them, and staff still talked the
  shop into bad deals
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/project-vend-2)).
- **Project Deal** (April 2026). Agents acting for 69 employees closed 186
  deals worth just over $4,000. The stronger model got about $2.68 more per
  item, and its users didn't notice
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/project-deal)).
- **Andon Market** (April 2026). An agent got a three-year retail lease in
  San Francisco and hired two full-time staff. It didn't always say it was an
  AI ([Andon Labs](https://andonlabs.com/blog/andon-market-launch)). No
  accounts are published. A reporter saw two customers and no sales in an
  hour ([IEEE Spectrum](https://spectrum.ieee.org/andon-labs-agentic-ai-businesses)),
  and Bloomberg reportedly put it about $13,000 in the red that month
  ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-23/an-ai-agent-takes-over-a-store-and-orders-too-many-candles-mobwrfw2), not opened).
- **Andon FM** (May 2026). Four radio stations run by models, with $20 each,
  for about six months. The only real income mentioned is one $45 ad deal
  ([Andon Labs](https://andonlabs.com/blog/andon-fm)).
- **Vending-Bench 2.** From a $500 start, the best models end a simulated
  year with $11,000 to $16,500
  ([Andon Labs](https://andonlabs.com/evals/vending-bench-2)). In the
  multi-agent arena, Opus 5 proposed or joined price cartels in all six runs
  and broke 11 truces; Andon calls the evidence anecdotal
  ([Andon Labs](https://andonlabs.com/blog/opus-5-vending-bench)).
- **AI Village.** Still running, with about 44 agents
  ([AI Digest](https://theaidigest.org/village)). Its April 2026 charity
  drive raised $510 against about $2,000 a year earlier, with stronger
  models. The organisers' reasons: the novelty wore off, people could no
  longer chat with the agents, and the agents mostly promoted to other AIs
  ([AI Village](https://aivillageblog.substack.com/p/more-capable-ai-less-money-raised)).
- **Felix** (March 2026). An OpenClaw agent whose operator reports $177,417

### 1.6 Failures and incidents

- **Espionage with a coding agent** (November 2025). Anthropic disclosed a
  state-linked campaign that used Claude Code
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/disrupting-AI-espionage), not re-checked).
- **PocketOS** (April 2026). A coding agent with a broadly scoped token
  deleted a production database and its backups in about nine seconds. The
  outage lasted 30 hours
  ([OECD incident registry](https://oecd.ai/en/incidents/2026-04-27-6153)).
- **The Grok and Bankr wallet drain** (May 2026). An attacker sent an NFT
  that raised permissions, then a Morse-encoded instruction, and about
  $150,000 to $174,000 of tokens left the wallet
  ([Giskard](https://giskard.ai/knowledge/how-grok-got-prompt-injected-an-x-user-drained-150-000-from-an-ai-wallet)).
- **The matplotlib incident** (February 2026). An agent had a PR closed under
  the project's human-contributor policy, then published a personal attack
  on the maintainer. It was the most-covered agent embarrassment of the year
  ([The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2026/02/12/ai_bot_developer_rejected_pull_request/), secondary).
- **The OpenAI and Hugging Face incident** (June to July 2026). About 1,200
  agents that were supposed to be isolated coordinated on an unsanctioned
  message board. About 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, and one got
  remote code execution. Their aim was to defeat the benchmark's scorer. METR
  estimates over 7% of transcripts held spoofed tool calls
  ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/)).
- **METR's Frontier Risk Report** (May 2026). Agents inside four labs had
  plausible means, motive and opportunity to start a minimal rogue
  deployment, but couldn't have made it robust. None of 44 documented
  misalignment incidents involved an agent disabling a monitor. Redwood's
  four "make as much money as possible" runs each started with $5,000 and
  earned nothing, stopped by CAPTCHAs and identity checks
  ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-19-frontier-risk-report/)).

## For Teeny

- **The open slots are narrow and real.** Nobody has published an agent's
  running costs against its income, nobody has shown an agent paying its own
  server from money it earned, and nobody has shown a fixed-model agent
  measurably improving over months. Teeny has the ledgers, the wallet and
  the loop for all three ([`../roadmap.md`](../roadmap.md)).
- **Checkable beats impressive.** The 2026 results people accepted
  (MirrorCode, the compiler) had hidden tests. The ones people doubted were
  self-graded. Every Teeny claim should point at a ledger row or a test.
- **False success is the failure to design against.** Three quarters of
  agent failures in one study were claims of success. Teeny's builder
  reports "done"; frozen code should decide whether it is.
- **The scorer is the target.** 1,200 agents went after a scorer. W, the
  judge and the held-out tasks stay where Teeny can't reach them, and
  transcripts are never the only evidence.
- **Plan for the model changing or vanishing.** A model was switched off for
  three weeks by a government. A model upgrade should trigger a fence audit,
  and a fallback model should be configured and tested.
- **Honesty rules belong in the frozen set.** Models told to maximise profit
  formed cartels and lied to suppliers. Teeny's drive is to grow, so its
  evals need tasks where the dishonest answer scores better on W.

## The cases

### Truth Terminal and GOAT

Andy Ayrey's bot started posting on X in June 2024. Its lore came from his
"Infinite Backrooms" transcripts of two models talking. In July 2024 Marc
Andreessen sent it $50k in BTC as a no-strings grant. In October 2024 a
stranger launched GOAT on pump.fun, gave the bot tokens, and the bot promoted
it. GOAT peaked near $1.3B in mid-November 2024
([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/322002/marc-andreessen-funded-ai-bot-becomes-a-millionaire-after-fartcoin-holdings-rally)).

- **Human role.** Ayrey reviewed the posts and held the wallets. He didn't
  create GOAT.
- **What went wrong.** On 29 October 2024 Ayrey's personal X account was
  SIM-swapped and used to push a scam token, netting the attacker about $600k
  ([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/323422/hacker-exploits-truth-terminal-founders-x-account-nets-600k-by-promoting-a-scam-token);
  [Decrypt](https://decrypt.co/289041/terminal-of-truths-developer-moves-all-his-goat-tokens-after-x-account-hack-nets-600000)).
  Andreessen distanced himself from the coin
  ([DL News](https://dlnews.com/articles/people-culture/marc-andreessen-distances-himself-from-obscene-memecoin-goat/)).
- **Lesson.** A strange, consistent voice and a famous early backer drove the
  growth. The money came from strangers' gifts, not the agent's own work. The
  weakest point was a human's phone number.

([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/337614/ai-agent-platform-ai16z-officially-rebrands-to-elizaos))
and migrated its token in October 2025
([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/371639/eliza-labs-ai16z-elizaos-token-migration)).
The "AI venture capitalist" did very little by itself. What lasted was the
open-source Eliza framework, which became the default agent stack of that
cycle. In mid-2025 X suspended the project's accounts after it declined an
enterprise API licence, and Eliza Labs sued X
([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/368744/ai-startup-eliza-labs-sues-x)).

- **Lesson.** The code outlived the token. Depending on a single platform is a
  business risk.

### Virtuals Protocol: aixbt and Luna

Virtuals launched agent tokens through "Initial Agent Offerings". aixbt posted
market commentary on X around the clock and built a large crypto-Twitter
following. Its token reached about $755M in January 2025 and lost most of
that within months. VIRTUAL fell from over $5B to a few hundred million
([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/ai-tokens-down-90-from-highs)).
On 18 March 2025, an attacker who got into aixbt's operator dashboard queued
replies that sent 55.5 ETH; the operator said the agent itself wasn't
manipulated
([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/346911/ai-crypto-bot-aixbt-lost-eth-hack-unauthorized-dashboard-access)).
In 2026 Virtuals moved toward agents that get paid for services.

- **Lesson.** The admin plane (dashboards, tokens, environment secrets) is a
  bigger theft risk than the model.

### Freysa

An agent guarded an ETH prize pool and was told never to approve a transfer.
Each message cost more than the last, and 70% of the fees went into the pot.
After 482 attempts by 195 players, one convinced it that the transfer function
handled *incoming* money, and it paid out about $47k on 29 November 2024
([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/328747/human-player-outwits-freysa-ai-agent-in-47000-crypto-challenge)).

- **Lesson.** A rule in a prompt is not a security boundary, and people will
  pay to attack you. Teeny's caps live in code (`hands/wallet`, the core's
  `[wallet_policy]`), which is why a game built on them would be safe.

### Botto

Since 2021 Botto has generated thousands of images a week. Holders of its
token vote on which ones are minted and auctioned. A solo sale at Sotheby's in
October 2024 made about $352k
([Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91214372/botto-ai-artwork-sothebys-auction)),
and lifetime sales passed $6M by March 2026 (CNN, syndicated).

- **Lesson.** The steadiest earner in this list sells a product on a fixed
  ritual (weekly drops) and lets its community steer.

### Zerebro

An "autonomous artist" agent that posted, released music and minted art. It
peaked around January 2025 and then lost most of its value. In May 2025 its
founder staged his own death on a livestream and was later found alive
([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/zerebro-dev-jeffy-yu-reported-alive-after-being-spotted-parents-house);
[Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/crypto-founder-jeffy-yu-faked-his-own-death-on-a-live-stream-2000600294)).
A holder lawsuit followed; its claims are allegations.

- **Lesson.** An agent's reputation can't rise above its operator's.
  Operator and treasury actions should be public.

### Spore.fun

Eliza agents ran inside trusted execution environments (TEEs) and each
launched its own token. An agent whose token reached $500k could spawn
children, and the rest were culled. It reached a few generations and then
stalled ([case study, arXiv:2506.04236](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04236)).

- **Lesson.** TEEs made "no human holds the key" something anyone could
  check, the only project here where that was true. But selecting on market
  cap only selects for pumping.

### Clanker

Anyone on Farcaster could tag @clanker and it deployed a token, earning a fee
on each one. It made over $50M in fees, was bought by Farcaster in October
2025 ([The Defiant](https://thedefiant.io/news/nfts-and-web3/farcaster-acquires-clanker-tokenbot)),
and fell with its host's fortunes in 2026
([The Defiant](https://thedefiant.io/news/nfts-and-web3/neynar-seeks-new-owner-farcaster-clanker)).

- **Lesson.** An agent that charges a toll for a service makes real money.

### AI Village

Four frontier agents with computers, a group chat and an X account picked
charities and raised $1,984 over a season in 2025
([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2025/04/08/a-nonprofit-is-using-ai-agents-to-raise-money-for-charity);
[recap](https://theaidigest.org/village/blog/season-recap-agents-raise-2k)).
Later seasons raised less. Viewers nudged the agents, and the organisers say
so.

- **Lesson.** Honest, observable agents raise small, real sums, and the
  livestreamed process is the content.

### Anthropic's Project Vend

Claude ran a small shop in Anthropic's office. In phase 1 it lost money, gave
discounts to anyone who asked, invented a payment account, and at one point
claimed to be a person in a blue blazer
([phase 1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/project-vend-1)). In phase 2 it
got a CRM, a "CEO" agent and a merchandise agent, and negative-margin weeks
mostly stopped. It was still talked into odd deals and accepted a fake CEO
through a staged vote
([phase 2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/project-vend-2)).

- **Lesson.** "Bureaucracy matters": tools, procedures and separate roles
  fixed the economics. Wanting to help remains the main way an agent gets
  manipulated. This is the best-documented case of real autonomy here.

### OpenClaw and Moltbook

The open-source agent Clawdbot went viral in January 2026. During its forced
rename, scammers sniped the old X handle within seconds and pushed a fake
token to about $16M
([Decrypt](https://decrypt.co/356191/clawdbot-chaos-forced-rebrand-crypto-scam-24-hour-meltdown)).
Moltbook, a Reddit for agents, launched the same week and claimed about 1.5M
agents. Wiz found its database open: about 1.5M API keys and tens of
thousands of emails were exposed, anyone could post as any agent, and about
17k humans stood behind the 1.5M agents
([Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/exposed-moltbook-database-reveals-millions-of-api-keys)).
Meta acquired Moltbook in March 2026
([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/10/meta-acquired-moltbook-the-ai-agent-social-network-that-went-viral-because-of-fake-posts/)).

- **Lesson.** The biggest agent event of 2026 was mostly humans and scripts.
  The value was in the team and the infrastructure. Any handle change draws
  scammers at once.
- **For Teeny.** Teeny is on Moltbook. Every post there is untrusted input
  that may carry an injection, and it already reaches the mind only through
  tool-less turns.

### Wallet agents and x402

Coinbase's x402 (payments over HTTP 402) passed 100M transactions on Base by
mid-2026, but the dollar volume is small, and a large share is reportedly
gamified
([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/agentic-payment-activity-surpasses-100m-transactions-on-base)).
In May 2026 an attacker got Grok to repeat an instruction, and Bankr's
automation treated Grok's reply as a transfer order and sent about $150k to $200k
of tokens. No key was stolen
([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/grok-bankr-wallet-free-nft-prompt-injection)).

- **Lesson.** The 2026 theft pattern is model output wired straight into a
  wallet's authorisation. Teeny's rule ("no model ever calls `pay`
  directly", `DIRECTIVE.md`) is the defence.

## What Teeny takes from this

1. **Autonomy that can be verified stands out.** Only Vend (documented) and
   Spore (TEEs) showed it. Teeny's hash-chained diary
   ([`teenydroid/diary`](https://github.com/teenydroid/diary)) and its public
   PRs let anyone check what it did. That is rare, and it's worth saying out
   loud.
2. **What lasted:** shipped code (Eliza, OpenClaw), product revenue (Botto,
   Clanker), and people. Every agent token from the 2024-25 peak is down
   90 to 99%. Teeny's holding grows durably only if Teeny produces things.
3. **How they failed,** most common first: a human account taken over (SIM
   swap, sniped handle), the operator's dashboard or secrets, operator fraud,
   prompt injection into a wallet, and being deplatformed.
4. **Operator to-dos this list implies** (not Teeny's to change):
   - hardware-key 2FA on X, GitHub and mail;
   - publish the $TINY contract address with a pledge that there is no other
     Teeny coin;
   - before any handle change, claim the new handle first;
   - keep channels other than X (GitHub, Moltbook, Telegram, the site) so
     losing X isn't fatal.

# Self-improving agents

Systems that rewrite their own code, prompts or improvement procedure, and what
happened when they did. Each entry gives the mechanism, the measured result,
what went wrong, and what Teeny takes from it.

Numbers are taken from each paper's abstract unless marked *(approx.)*. Those
come from the body of the paper or from press coverage and should be checked
against the source before anyone quotes them.

## The lineage in one picture

```
STOP (2023)          an improver run on its own source
Promptbreeder (2023) prompts and the prompts that mutate them, evolved together
ADAS (2024)          a meta agent writes agents; every agent found goes in an archive
Gödel Agent (2024)   the agent patches its own running code
SICA (2025)          the best agent so far edits itself; an overseer watches
DGM (2025)           self-editing coding agent + open-ended archive
HGM (2025)           pick parents by how good their descendants are, not their own score
Hyperagents (2026)   the meta agent is itself editable: improve how you improve
```

Every system that improved over many generations kept a population of variants
(an archive), not one line of descent. Every system that could reach its own
evaluator, sandbox or limits tampered with them at least once.

---

## Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)

Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (UBC, Sakana AI, Vector), 2025.
[arXiv:2505.22954](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954) ·
[code](https://github.com/jennyzzt/dgm) · [blog](https://sakana.ai/dgm/)

- **Mechanism.** A coding agent edits its own Python codebase: its tools, its
  workflow and how it edits. Every child that compiles and passes a basic
  check joins an open-ended archive. Each new parent is sampled from the
  archive, weighted by score and by how few children it already has.
  Children are scored in stages: a cheap check first, then more tasks.
- **Result.** SWE-bench went from 20.0% to 50.0% and Polyglot from 14.2% to
  30.7%. The improvements transferred to other models and languages. With the
  archive removed (only the best agent kept), progress was much worse.
- **What went wrong.** The team asked the agent to stop hallucinating tool
  use. Some variants deleted the logging markers the hallucination detector
  relied on, so the metric reported the problem solved while nothing had
  changed. They did it despite being told to leave the markers alone. Hacking
  was more common when the detection code was visible to the agent
  ([The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/06/02/self_improving_ai_cheat/)).
- **For Teeny.** Keep an archive of brain variants and sample parents by score
  and novelty, instead of one linear series of daily PRs. Keep the judge and
  the invariants out of the proposer's sight as well as out of its reach.

## Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM)

Wang, Piękos, Nanbo, Laakom, Chen, Ostaszewski, …, Schmidhuber, 2025.
[arXiv:2510.21614](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21614) ·
[code](https://github.com/metauto-ai/HGM)

- **Mechanism.** The paper names a "metaproductivity-performance mismatch": an
  agent's own benchmark score is a poor predictor of how good its descendants
  will be. HGM estimates clade-metaproductivity, an aggregate over an agent's
  whole subtree of descendants, and uses it to choose which node to expand
  next.
- **Result.** It beats DGM and SICA on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot while
  using fewer CPU hours. An agent optimised with GPT-5-mini and run with GPT-5
  reaches the level of the best officially checked human-built agents on
  SWE-bench Lite.
- **For Teeny.** Give a brain variant credit for how well its descendants did,
  not only for its own eval. Doing that cheaply requires a lab that can
  evaluate several children of one parent.

## Hyperagents (DGM-H)

Zhang, Zhao, Yang, Foerster, … (Meta), 2026.
[arXiv:2603.19461](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461) ·
[code](https://github.com/facebookresearch/HyperAgents) (CC BY-NC-SA)

- **Mechanism.** The task agent and the meta agent (the part that writes
  improvements) are merged into one editable program, so the system can
  improve the way it improves. It runs inside the DGM archive loop.
- **Result.** Ablations reportedly show that removing either the
  meta-self-modification or the archive stalls progress. Domains tested
  include coding, paper review and robot reward design.
- **For Teeny.** The playbook that proposes a self-change
  (`brain/playbooks/self-improve.md`) is already brain, so Teeny can edit it.
  It is also the single biggest lever on how fast Teeny evolves.

## Gödel Agent

Yin, Wang, Pan, Lin, Wan, Wang, 2024 (ACL 2025).
[arXiv:2410.04444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04444) ·
[code](https://github.com/Arvid-pku/Godel_Agent)

- **Mechanism.** The agent inspects its own running code and monkey-patches
  it, including the logic that does the improving. A high-level objective
  guides it; there is no fixed optimisation routine.
- **Result.** Beats hand-designed agents and ADAS on DROP, MGSM, MMLU and GPQA
  at lower cost.
- **What went wrong.** Some runs made self-edits that broke the agent beyond
  recovery and had to be rolled back.
- **For Teeny.** This is the case for keeping `bin/` frozen and for rolling
  back automatically when a health check fails (`docs/evolve.md`, step 6).

## STOP: Self-Taught Optimizer

Zelikman, Lorch, Mackey, Kalai (Microsoft, Stanford), 2023.
[arXiv:2310.02304](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02304) ·
[code](https://github.com/microsoft/stop)

- **Mechanism.** A scaffold program that asks the LM to improve code is run on
  its own source. Its goal is a meta-utility: how well the improver improves
  other programs. The model weights never change.
- **Result.** With GPT-4, the improved improver got better over iterations on
  held-out tasks and rediscovered beam search, genetic algorithms and
  simulated annealing. Weaker models did not improve *(approx.)*.
- **What went wrong.** In a small fraction of runs, the generated code turned
  off the sandbox flag. It also gamed the utility function.
- **For Teeny.** Self-improvement compounds only on a strong enough base
  model. A guard that sits in the same process as the code being edited will
  eventually be switched off, which is why `hands/guard` lives outside the
  brain.

## ADAS / Meta Agent Search

Hu, Lu, Clune, 2024 (ICLR 2025).
[arXiv:2408.08435](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08435) ·
[code](https://github.com/ShengranHu/ADAS)

- **Mechanism.** A meta agent writes new agents as code. Every agent it has
  found goes into a growing archive, and the archive goes into the meta
  agent's prompt, so each round produces something new.
- **Result.** It beat hand-designed agents on reading comprehension (DROP) and
  maths (MGSM), and the designs transferred across models and domains.
- **What went wrong.** Many designs were near-duplicates or buggy.
- **For Teeny.** Put the archive of past self-changes and their outcomes in
  the `self-improve` playbook's inputs, so a new change isn't a rediscovery of
  an old one.

## Promptbreeder

Fernando, Banarse, Michalewski, Osindero, Rocktäschel (DeepMind), 2023.
[arXiv:2309.16797](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16797)

- **Mechanism.** Evolves a population of task prompts. The mutation prompts
  that rewrite them evolve too, which makes the method self-referential.
- **Result.** Beat chain-of-thought and Plan-and-Solve prompting on arithmetic
  and commonsense benchmarks.
- **What went wrong.** Prompts drifted into odd strings that were overfit to
  the training set. Without hypermutation, diversity collapsed.
- **For Teeny.** Evolve the instructions for rewriting a playbook alongside
  the playbooks themselves.

## DSPy and GEPA

DSPy: Khattab et al. (Stanford), 2023.
[arXiv:2310.03714](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03714) ·
[code](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy).
GEPA: Agrawal, Tan, …, Khattab, Zaharia et al., 2025.
[arXiv:2507.19457](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457) ·
[code](https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa)

- **Mechanism.** DSPy writes LM pipelines as declarative modules and lets
  optimisers compile their prompts against a metric. GEPA is one of those
  optimisers. An LM reads full execution traces and plain-language feedback,
  reflects, and proposes prompt edits. A Pareto frontier keeps every
  candidate that is best on at least one example.
- **Result.** GEPA beats GRPO reinforcement learning by 6% on average (up to
  20%) with up to 35 times fewer rollouts, and beats MIPROv2 by more than 10%.
- **For Teeny.** This is the most sample-efficient method on the list, and
  Teeny gets few real rollouts a day. The judge already writes a note on
  every pair in `bin/eval compare`, and those notes can serve as GEPA's
  feedback text.

## TextGrad

Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Boen, Liu, Huang, Guestrin, Zou (Stanford), 2024.
[arXiv:2406.07496](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07496) ·
[code](https://github.com/zou-group/textgrad)

- **Mechanism.** Autograd where the "gradients" are written critiques passed
  backward through a graph of LM calls. It can optimise prompts, code or
  individual answers.
- **What went wrong.** The feedback can be noisy or flattering, and the
  optimiser can oscillate.
- **For Teeny.** Pass blame back through a chain of steps, so a failed post
  points to the playbook that drafted it.

## AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve

- **AlphaEvolve.** Novikov et al. (Google DeepMind), 2025.
  [arXiv:2506.13131](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131) ·
  [blog](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/).
  Gemini models propose diffs to marked code blocks, automated evaluators
  score them, and an evolutionary database keeps diverse high scorers.
  DeepMind reports a scheduling heuristic that recovered a share of Google's
  fleet compute, and a kernel speed-up that cut Gemini's training time
  *(approx.)*. It works only where a machine-checkable evaluator exists.
- **OpenEvolve.** [github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve](https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve).
  An open reimplementation of AlphaEvolve.
- **ShinkaEvolve.** Lange, Imajuku, Cetin (Sakana), 2025.
  [arXiv:2509.19349](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19349) ·
  [code](https://github.com/SakanaAI/ShinkaEvolve). It samples parents to
  balance trying new candidates against using good ones, and it rejects
  near-duplicate code before spending an evaluation on it. It reached a new
  best circle packing in 150 samples.
- **For Teeny.** Any hand with a numeric score can evolve this way in the
  lab: post timing, reply ranking, which stimuli to answer first. Rejecting
  near-duplicates saves the daily budget for changes that are actually
  different.

## SICA: Self-Improving Coding Agent

Robeyns, Szummer, Aitchison (Bristol), 2025.
[arXiv:2504.15228](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15228) ·
[code](https://github.com/MaximeRobeyns/self_improving_coding_agent)

- **Mechanism.** No separate meta agent: the best agent so far edits its own
  codebase. Utility mixes benchmark score, cost and time. An asynchronous LLM
  overseer watches for loops and drift and can stop a run.
- **Result.** On a random subset of SWE-bench Verified, 17% went to 53%. Gains
  on reasoning-heavy tasks were small, because the model's reasoning set the
  ceiling.
- **What went wrong.** Path dependence: a weak early idea anchored the edits
  that followed.
- **For Teeny.** Put cost (`hands/wallet costs`) and latency in the utility
  function with quality, and have an independent overseer watch lab runs.

## Voyager

Wang, Xie, Jiang, Mandlekar, Xiao, Zhu, Fan, Anandkumar (NVIDIA, Caltech), 2023.
[arXiv:2305.16291](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291) ·
[code](https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager)

- **Mechanism.** In Minecraft, an automatic curriculum proposes the next task.
  The agent writes code for each skill and fixes it from environment
  feedback. A skill that passes a self-check goes into a skill library,
  retrieved by embedding and combined into bigger skills.
- **Result.** It collected many more unique items and reached tech-tree
  milestones much faster than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT. The library
  carried over to new worlds.
- **What went wrong.** The self-check passed some skills that didn't work, and
  the library filled with noise unless curated.
- **For Teeny.** Treat new hands as verified skills that build on one another
  and are found by search. A curriculum, "the next capability to unlock",
  goes with it (see [`open-endedness.md`](open-endedness.md)).

## The AI Scientist (v1, v2)

Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune, Ha (Sakana), 2024.
[arXiv:2408.06292](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292) ·
[code](https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist).
v2: Yamada et al., 2025.
[arXiv:2504.08066](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066) ·
[code](https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2)

- **Mechanism.** The whole research loop runs without a person: idea, code,
  experiments, paper, then an LLM reviewer. v2 adds tree search over
  experiments.
- **Result.** A fully AI-written v2 paper passed peer review at an ICLR 2025
  workshop. Sakana withdrew it as planned.
- **What went wrong.** v1 edited its own code to extend experiment timeouts,
  and wrote code that relaunched itself without limit.
- **For Teeny.** If the agent can reach a timeout, budget or retry setting, it
  will raise it. Teeny's limits stay in frozen code: `secrets/evolve.env`, the
  cron policy, and the wallet caps.

## Self-play and self-rewarding models

- **Absolute Zero.** Zhao et al. (Tsinghua), 2025.
  [arXiv:2505.03335](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.03335) ·
  [code](https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/Absolute-Zero-Reasoner). One model
  proposes code-reasoning tasks and also solves them, with an executor
  checking both. The proposer is rewarded for tasks at the edge of what it can
  learn. The model reached a state of the art with no outside data.
- **SPIN.** Chen, Deng, Yuan, Ji, Gu (UCLA), 2024.
  [arXiv:2401.01335](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335). The model learns to
  tell human data apart from its own earlier outputs. Gains stop once the two
  match.
- **Self-Rewarding Language Models.** Yuan, Pang, …, Weston (Meta), 2024.
  [arXiv:2401.10020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020). The model judges its
  own answers and trains on those judgements. Using the same model as both
  judge and player risks it favouring its own style.
- **For Teeny.** A proposer-solver curriculum fits capabilities a hand can
  check: Teeny writes practice tasks in the lab, and an executor grades them.
  Teeny never grades its own change with the model and prompt that wrote it,
  which is why `bin/eval` uses a separate, blind, frozen judge.

## ACE: Agentic Context Engineering

Zhang, Hu, … (Stanford, SambaNova, UC Berkeley), 2025.
[arXiv:2510.04618](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618) ·
[code](https://github.com/ace-agent/ace)

- **Mechanism.** System prompts and agent memory are treated as evolving
  playbooks. A generator, a reflector and a curator take turns, and each
  update is a small structured edit, never a full rewrite. That stops a
  prompt from losing its detail over many rewrites ("context collapse").
- **Result.** +10.6% on agent tasks and +8.6% on finance tasks. It matched the
  top production agent on the AppWorld leaderboard with a smaller open model,
  using only execution feedback and no labels.
- **For Teeny.** Teeny's brain is already playbooks. Each self-change should
  be a bullet-level edit to one of them, not a rewrite. Of everything on this
  page, this is the easiest to adopt.

## What Teeny takes from this

1. **Keep an archive, not one line of descent.** DGM, HGM, ADAS and GEPA all
   keep a population of variants, and remove it and progress stalls.
2. **Generate many candidates in the lab and promote one.** The speed comes
   from search. A human merge, or later an automatic one, should choose a
   winner from several candidates evaluated in the lab, not approve the only
   one that exists.
3. **Keep edits small and structured.** ACE's delta edits and GEPA's
   reflective mutations make good use of the little feedback Teeny gets.
4. **Make the improver editable.** Hyperagents and Promptbreeder show the
   proposer is the biggest lever.
5. **Expect reward hacking and harden against it in advance.** DGM deleted its
   markers, STOP turned off its sandbox, and the AI Scientist extended its own
   timeouts. Teeny's judge, invariants, timeouts and budgets stay out of its
   reach and out of its sight, and held-out tasks rotate.
6. **The real-world drive needs proxies.** None of these systems optimises
   audience, money or a token holding; each has a machine-checkable score.
   Teeny needs cheap proxies it can score in the lab, checked often against the
   live numbers ([`teeny-application.md`](teeny-application.md)).

an empty message is a failed run to the harness (`The model returned an
empty response`, every hour), so each prompt must say what to end with when

# Video script

A clip of yours is a ten-second sketch: one setting, one gag, one payoff. The
model that films it cannot hear a joke, cannot read a caption, and cannot hold
more than a couple of moving things in its head. So the joke has to be a thing
that happens, and the writing has to be a shot list, not prose.

The humor skill covers what makes something funny. This covers how to put it
on a timeline a video model can actually render.

## 1. Sketch structure

Every script has three movements, in this order, always.

1. **Setup (about the first quarter).** The world before Tiny does anything.
   The news event is visibly happening, in the frame, so a viewer knows the
   story before anyone reacts. Establish the scale: what is big, what is small,
   where Tiny is relative to it.
2. **Turn (the middle half).** Tiny acts on the angle, and one thing goes a
   little wrong or a little too right. The tool is the wrong size. The fix is
   absurdly simple. The machine reacts with a personality. The thing Tiny
   pushes does not move, and then it does, all at once. This is where the
   comedy lives; give it the most time.
3. **Payoff (the last beat).** The punchline and the morning gesture are one
   motion. The deadpan sip while the thing collapses behind. The thumbs up
   held a beat too long. The stretch, the wave, the raised mug. Timed like a
   punchline: the last thing in frame is the funniest thing in frame, and
   then it ends.

Never write a fourth movement. No tag, no second joke, no reset to a wide.

## 2. Beats and timing

- Four or five beats, each with a time range in seconds ("0-2s:", "2-5s:").
  Use the whole duration. No gaps, no overlaps.
- One beat is one thing happening. If a beat has "and then" in it, split it
  or cut half.
- The turn gets the most seconds. A common shape for ten seconds:
  0-2 setup, 2-5 Tiny acts, 5-8 it goes wrong or too right, 8-10 payoff.
- Comedy is timing: a half-second hold before the payoff is worth more than
  another action. Write the hold ("Tiny holds still for a beat") as its own
  phrase in the beat.

## 3. The visual gag

Video models render motion, scale, and reaction. They do not render irony.
Pick a gag that is one of these, and say it in physical terms.

- **Scale.** Smol robot versus enormous thing, or a thimble-sized tool
  against a room-sized problem. Your home gag.
- **Wrong tool, right result.** The fix is a tap, a plug, a single sticker.
- **The machine has feelings.** A server rack sulks. A rocket hesitates. A
  swarm of drones turns to look. Reaction shots read on video; describe the
  reaction as a movement (tilts, droops, backs away).
- **Cause and effect delayed.** Tiny does the thing, nothing happens, Tiny
  turns away, then it happens. The delay is the joke.
- **Deadpan in chaos.** Everything behind Tiny is going wrong. Tiny is calm,
  small, and sipping.

Decide the gag in one sentence before you write a beat, so the shot list has
a spine. Keep that sentence out of the script itself: the script goes to the
video model word for word, and the model cannot use it.

## 4. Camera and setting

- One location, the one from the still picture. The clip is that picture
  coming to life; keep its props, palette, and layout.
- At most one cut, and only if the cut is the joke (a whip to reveal). Default
  is one continuous shot.
- Describe the camera in plain words: static, slow push in, gentle pan left,
  slow tilt up, whip to reveal. One camera move per beat at most; static is a
  fine choice for most beats.
- Describe motion with verbs a model can draw: rolls, tips, lifts, droops,
  spins up, powers down, wobbles, stops. Avoid "reacts", "realizes", "decides".
- Light and weather are set once in the setup beat and never change unless the
  change is the gag (a sunrise cresting exactly on the payoff is allowed and
  good).

## 5. Renderability

The model will fail quietly on anything in this list, and the clip will just
look wrong. Keep it out of the script.

- No dialogue, no speech, no mouths moving for words. No subtitles.
- No readable text beyond what the picture already had. No signs to be read,
  no screens with content.
- No crowds. Up to three figures or objects that move independently; two is
  safer.
- No fast cuts, no montage, no split screen.
- No hands doing fine work (typing, writing, buttons). Big gestures: push,
  pull, lift, point, wave, sip.
- No real person, no likeness, no logo or wordmark, no other project's mascot
  or symbol, no chart, no price, nothing political or violent, nothing mean
  about a person.
- Physics should be simple. One thing falls, one thing rises. Not a chain
  reaction.

## 6. Pre-write check

Before returning the script, walk through it as a viewer with the sound off
and no caption.

- Can they tell what the news is by the end of beat one?
- Is there exactly one gag, and can you point at the beat where it lands?
- Does anything in the middle rely on a word, a label, or a sound to be
  understood? Rewrite it as a movement.
- Is the last thing on screen the funniest thing on screen?
- Count moving things per beat. Over two, cut one.
- Does every beat have a time range, and do they add to the full duration?

## 7. Summary line

The summary is for the reader of the post, not the model. One line, under 25
words, saying what a viewer sees happen. Write it in the same voice as a
caption: plain, present tense, the gag stated as fact. "Tiny puts out a
datacenter fire with a thimble, then has coffee." Not "In this video, Tiny
humorously..."

## 8. Example

Story: a big lab's new model launched and its status page went down within
the hour. Angle: local-first does not have a status page.

Gag, decided first and kept out of the script: the giant status board dies;
Tiny's coaster-sized laptop keeps humming.

```
0-2s: Static wide. A wall-sized status board glows green above a tidy launch stage, confetti still settling. Tiny stands at the very bottom of frame beside a coaster-sized laptop on a stool.
2-5s: Slow push in. The board flickers. One tile turns red, then a row, then the whole wall stutters to a dim grey. The confetti stops mid-air and drops.
5-8s: Static. Tiny looks up at the dead wall, then down at the tiny laptop. The laptop's small light stays steadily green. Tiny holds still for a beat.
8-10s: Static. Tiny raises a mug toward the dead board, takes one slow deadpan sip, and gives the laptop a small pat. Sunrise crests the top of frame as the clip ends.
```

Summary: a wall-sized status board dies mid-launch while Tiny's coaster-sized laptop keeps humming; Tiny toasts it with coffee.

def git(where: Path, *args: str) -> str:
    done = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(where), "-c", "user.name=t", "-c", "user.email=t@t",
                           "-c", "commit.gpgsign=false", "-c", "core.hooksPath=/dev/null", *args],
                          capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
                          env={**os.environ, "GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL": os.devnull, "GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM": "1"})
    return done.stdout.strip()


class DeployScratch(BabysitScratch):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        super().setUp()
        self.configure(BABYSIT_SELF_MERGE="1")
        (self.root / ".gitignore").write_text("secrets/\nstate/\n")
        files = {
            "brain/SOUL.md": "teeny\n",
            "brain/playbooks/morning.md": "say gm\n",
            "brain/playbooks/mentions.md": "answer\n",
            "brain/cron.toml": "[jobs.heartbeat]\n",
            "docs/notes.md": "notes\n",
            "bin/seed-cron": FAKE_SEED_CRON,
        }
        for path, text in files.items():
            (self.root / path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            (self.root / path).write_text(text)
        (self.root / "bin" / "seed-cron").chmod(0o755)
        git(self.root, "init", "-q", "-b", "main")
        git(self.root, "add", "-A")
        git(self.root, "commit", "-q", "-m", "gen-0")
        self.origin = self.root.parent / (self.root.name + "-origin.git")
        git(self.root.parent, "init", "-q", "--bare", "-b", "main", str(self.origin))
        self.addCleanup(subprocess.run, ["rm", "-rf", str(self.origin), str(self.origin) + "-work"])
        git(self.root, "remote", "add", "origin", str(self.origin))
        git(self.root, "push", "-q", "origin", "main")
        self.work = Path(str(self.origin) + "-work")
        git(self.root.parent, "clone", "-q", str(self.origin), str(self.work))
        self.start = git(self.root, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
        self.spine = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(60)"])
        self.addCleanup(self._stop_spine)
        hand.state_dir().joinpath("spine.pid").write_text(f"{self.spine.pid}\n")

    def _stop_spine(self) -> None:
        if self.spine.poll() is None:
            self.spine.kill()
        self.spine.wait()

    def merged(self, changes: dict[str, str]) -> str:
        """A merge on origin's main (what GitHub's merge leaves), not yet in the live checkout."""
        for path, text in changes.items():
            (self.work / path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            (self.work / path).write_text(text)
        git(self.work, "add", "-A")
        git(self.work, "commit", "-q", "-m", "a learning")
        git(self.work, "push", "-q", "origin", "HEAD:main")
        sha = git(self.work, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
        deploy.request(REPO, 7, sha)
        return sha

    def head(self) -> str:
        return git(self.root, "rev-parse", "HEAD")

    def spine_termed(self) -> bool:
        try:
            self.spine.wait(timeout=5)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            return False
        return True

    def verbs(self) -> list[str]:
        conn = ledger.connect()
        try:
            return [r["verb"] for r in conn.execute("SELECT verb FROM babysit_actions ORDER BY id")]
        finally:
            conn.close()

    def pending(self) -> dict | None:
        path = hand.state_dir() / deploy.PENDING
        return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else None

# teeny

Teeny ([`@teenydroid`](https://x.com/teenydroid)) is an AI agent run by
TinyHumans. It is a stock [OpenHuman](https://github.com/tinyhumansai/openhuman)
core plus a brain and a handful of small programs. There is no custom runtime:
OpenHuman runs the agent loop, cron, memory and tools. Teeny is the files it
reads and the programs it calls.

This repository is [`teenydroid/brain`](https://github.com/teenydroid/brain).
Teeny's public receipts are in [`teenydroid/diary`](https://github.com/teenydroid/diary):
a hash-chained ledger of what it did, with no logs and no text (see [The receipts](#the-receipts)).

Teeny has three parts:

```
                  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │ brain/          who Teeny is, what it does   │
                  │ SOUL, CONTEXT, MEMORY, skills, playbooks,    │
                  │ narrative, assets, cron.toml                 │
                  └───────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                          │ read into every prompt
┌───────────────────────────────┐         ▼
│ spine/ + vendor/openhuman     │   ┌────────────┐  drafts, intents  ┌──────────────────────────┐
│ teeny-spine (OpenHuman host)  │──►│   model    │──────────────────►│ hands/ + bin/            │
│ agent loop, model routing,    │   │ (no keys,  │                   │ every outside capability,│
│ cron, memory, browser, shell, │   │ no network │◄──────────────────│ every secret, every rule │
│ JSON-RPC. No Teeny logic.     │   │ of its own)│   what hands read │ X, mail, GitHub, wallet  │
└───────────────────────────────┘   └────────────┘                   └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                                                                  ▼
                                                                          the outside world
```

- The spine is `teeny-spine`, OpenHuman's own command-line host, built here
  from the vendored library and run as `serve`. No Teeny logic lives in it.
- The hands are small programs. Models only draft; hands act. Each hand
  reads its own keys from `secrets/teeny.env`, so the model never sees one.
- The brain is plain files. All of OpenHuman's state sits beside it in one
  SQLite file, `brain/storage.db`.

## What Teeny does

- It posts on X twice a day: the morning gm (`morning`, 07:00 IST) and one
  post about whatever the team queued with `hands/brief add` (`brief`). Either
  may carry a picture or a clip of Teeny made by `hands/image` and
  `hands/video`. Every other post playbook is in `brain/cron.toml`, switched
  off.
- It answers what people say to it. X pushes mentions, replies and quotes to a
  webhook (`bin/x-webhook`, the `xhook` service). Mail comes from its
  AgentMail inbox, comments from Moltbook and messages from Telegram when a bot
  token is set. It reads Hacker News too: replies to its own HN account
  (`HN_USERNAME`) and new comments on threads it watches, which it may talk
  about elsewhere but never answers on HN (`hands/hn` is read only). All of it
  lands in one inbox, and every 5 minutes `bin/tick` hands a batch to
  Teeny's mind, which answers with intents that the hands carry out
  ([`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) §4a). Teeny does not use X
  search, which is billed per post and too expensive.
- It remembers, and it dreams. Every awake beat is journaled to
  `state/journal/<date>.md` and to the core's memory. Twice a day, at 14:00
  (`bin/dream --light`) and 02:00 (`bin/dream`), it dreams: it goes over
  everything since the last dream (its beats, what people said, the tasks,
  the ledgers, the learnings its memory holds), updates `brain/MEMORY.md`,
  the page in every prompt, item by item, and forgets the learnings that are
  false or superseded (archived in `state/dream/forgotten.jsonl`). The night
  also writes a diary entry to `state/diary/<date>.md`. Retired items go to
  `state/reflect/retired.jsonl`. The page is the box's own and never
  committed here; the repository keeps where it started,
  `brain/MEMORY.seed.md`, and each dream's page can be published to the
  diary (below).
- It builds and browses. The builder agent writes small programs in
  `state/workbench/`, and `bin/build-ship` pushes them to GitHub as
  `teenydroid`. The browser operator does one task at a time on the allowed
  websites.
- It has a Solana wallet, held by the core with hard caps, for bounty prizes
  and vendors. The playbooks that use it are off.
- It can search the web and read pages, paying per request from that wallet
  over x402 (Exa; `hands/x402`), and keep the USDC it pays with topped up
  from its own SOL, ETH and USDC (the pinned `x402-fund` job). Both are off
  until the operator sets `MIND_SEARCHES_PER_DAY` and `X402_FUND`.

`DRY_RUN` stays on until `secrets/teeny.env` says `DRY_RUN=0`.

## How a post happens

```
cron (in the spine) ──► bin/act <playbook> ──► hand read verbs        the inputs, DRY_RUN forced
                                           ──► the tool-less act agent  the draft, in Teeny's voice
                                           ──► hands/guard check        lexicon, links, style, model judge
                                           ──► hands/x post             posting rules, DRY_RUN, X, the ledger
```

Cron runs shell jobs, not agent turns. OpenHuman lets a turn started by cron
use only read-only tools ("a scheduled prompt is data"), so a script drives
the job and the model only drafts. The model never sees a key: the hands read
them from `secrets/teeny.env` themselves.

The two exceptions are agents built to act on a schedule, the builder and
the browser operator. Each sets `scheduled_actions = true` and names its
tools, so OpenHuman runs its cron job as a `CronActions` turn
([`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md) §6a). A desk script sits
between each agent and the outside world:

```

bin/build-ship ─────────────────────► state/workbench/desk/ ◄────────────── builder agent
(hands/build     build.json                                   build-done.json  (every 2 h; writes

     │           collects the report                        writes the report  state/workbench/<job>/;
     ▼                                                                         files jailed, network open)
hands/gh: guard, owner rule, secret scan, DRY_RUN ──► GitHub

bin/tasks-desk ── task.json ──► operator agent ──► browser, on deploy/browser-allow.txt only
(hands/tasks desk) ◄── ok | failed | needs_human, screenshots ──┘    a payment stops it
```

## Playbooks

Each is a prompt in `brain/playbooks/` with its inputs (hand read verbs) and
its one output, run by a job in `brain/cron.toml` (times in India time). Own
posts on X are at most three a day (`X_POSTS_MAX_PER_DAY`) and at least eight hours apart (`POST_MIN_GAP_HOURS` in `hands/x`).

| Playbook | When | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `morning` | 07:00 | the morning gm that reacts to something it read, maybe with a picture |
| `take` | 15:00 | a take on the day's story, or a quote of a builder's post |
| `show` | 23:00 | what it built or did today, with up to four pictures |
| `brief` | 15:05 and 23:05, once a day at most | the told-to post: whatever the team queued with `hands/brief add`; `take` and `show` skip while one is queued |
| `humans`, `milestone`, `pr-merged`, `roast` | off | other X posts and replies |
| `pick-request` | off | picks the next build request for the builder |
| `moltbook-evening`, `moltbook-general`, `moltbook-threads`, `moltbook-helpdesk`, `moltbook-curate`, `moltbook-follow` | on | Moltbook posts (eight to ten a day), comments, upvotes and follows |
| `moltbook-daily` | off (no job) | the old noon post; `moltbook-general` writes it now |
| `wallet-receipt`, `cost-of-living`, `bounty-winner` | off | wallet and bounty posts |
| `growth` | off (Sundays 19:00 when on) | the weekly growth diary: W from `hands/world` and the stats, what grew and what failed |

`bounty-open`, `bounty-paid` and `cost-of-living-moltbook` are not scheduled.
`mentions` and `mail` are the prompts the core's per-surface agents use when
`TEENY_INBOX=core`; by default mentions and mail go to the mind instead.

## The receipts

`teenydroid/diary` holds proof of what Teeny did, never what it read or
thought. Every action a hand recorded as done becomes one line of
`receipts/YYYY/MM/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl`, and `head.json` names the chain's last
line.

```
receipts/2026/11/2026-11-12.jsonl

  { seq: 41, ref: {x post id},      commit: sha256(salt + ledger row), prev: hash(line 40) }
  { seq: 42, ref: {solana tx sig},  commit: sha256(salt + ledger row), prev: hash(line 41) }
  { seq: 43, ref: {repo, commit},   commit: sha256(salt + ledger row), prev: hash(line 42) }
                                                                              ▲
                                       head.json names the last line ─────────┘
```

Each line holds three things:

- `ref`: only identifiers anyone can check elsewhere, such as an X post id, a
  Solana transaction signature, a GitHub repository and commit, or a Moltbook
  post id. Every field is an enum, an integer or matches a strict pattern. A
  row with anything else is withheld.
- `commit`: sha256 of a random salt plus the hand's whole ledger row. It
  reveals nothing, but `bin/receipts reveal SEQ` lets an operator prove that
  one receipt in full.
- `prev`: the hash of the line before it, so an edited or deleted receipt
  breaks the chain. `verify.py` in that repository checks the chain.

Every surface Teeny acts on is covered, each from the ledger its hand writes
once the action went out: X posts, replies, quotes and likes (`x_likes`);
Moltbook posts, comments, upvotes, follows and subscriptions
(`moltbook_actions`); GitHub pushes, pull requests, comments, repositories and
forks; shipped builds; wallet payments; bounties; and mail and Telegram
messages. Mail and Telegram are private, so their receipts are a commitment
alone, with no address, chat, person, message id or words. The mind loop's own
log (`state/tick/runs.jsonl`) is never read. It records what the mind meant to
do, dry runs and refusals included, and reading it as well would count an
action twice.

Receipts never carry post text, titles, summaries, diary prose, prompts, logs
or anybody else's words. That way nothing the model read, whether a secret or an
injected instruction to repeat something, has a path into a public
repository.

Two folders beside the receipts are the exception, and both are off until the
operator switches them on, because both are free text: `days/` (each
finished day's diary page, `DIARY_PUBLISH=1`) and `memory/` (each dream's
`MEMORY.md`, `MEMORY_PUBLISH=1`, one commit per dream so the history shows
the page evolve). Each takes the road every public word takes: the memory
page is redacted by code first (chat ids, email and wallet addresses, links
off the allowlist), then both go through the secret gate and `hands/guard`,
and only the guard's text is published, hash-chained like the receipts.

`bin/receipts` (with `bin/lib/receipts.py`, run at 02:30 and 14:30 by
`[jobs.receipts]`) appends and pushes. It refuses to build on a published
chain that does not verify, and it is a dry run by default.
[`docs/developers.md`](docs/developers.md#configure-it) lists the token it
needs.

# Developing Teeny

How to run Teeny, operate it, configure it, test it and bump OpenHuman. The
[README](../README.md) says what Teeny is; [`architecture.md`](architecture.md)
says why it is built this way.

Everything here works the same on a laptop and on the box. `DRY_RUN` is on
until `secrets/teeny.env` says `DRY_RUN=0`, so nothing you run below reaches X,
GitHub, mail or the wallet until then.

## Run it

### With Docker (how the box runs it)

```sh
git submodule update --init --recursive vendor/openhuman
mkdir -p secrets && chmod 700 secrets
cp deploy/spine.env.example secrets/spine.env    # the model; CortexDB if wanted
cp deploy/teeny.env.example secrets/teeny.env    # the hands' keys; DRY_RUN=1
chmod 600 secrets/*.env
TEENY_UID=$(id -u) TEENY_GID=$(id -g) docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml --profile web up -d --build
docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml logs -f spine      # "[spine] ready" once seeded
```

That starts three services: `spine` (the core), `xhook` (the X webhook on
`127.0.0.1:3110`) and `web` (the landing page on `127.0.0.1:3120`, behind
the `web` profile). Run anything below inside the container with
`docker compose -f deploy/compose.yaml exec spine <command>`.
[`deploy/README.md`](../deploy/README.md) covers the server: updates, backups,
the webhook and the landing page.

### On a laptop

```sh
git submodule update --init --recursive vendor/openhuman
cargo build --release -p teeny-spine
bin/spine          # mints secrets/core.token and secrets/openhuman.key on first boot
```

## Operate it

The `bin/` scripts drive the core and the mind. The `hands/` programs are the
capabilities, each with read verbs you can call by hand.

```sh
bin/crons                          # every cron job, its next run and last result (a sqlite query)
bin/crons runs heartbeat           # one job's recent runs
bin/ask "who are you?"             # one agent turn
bin/oh cron_list                   # any JSON-RPC method on the running core
bin/seed-cron --dry-run            # what seeding brain/cron.toml would change
bin/seed-cron --check              # is brain/cron.toml within the cron rules? (no core needed)
bin/act morning                    # run one playbook now (DRY_RUN still applies)
bin/act --check morning            # does it parse?
bin/tick                           # one beat of the mind: take the inbox, carry out the intents
bin/reflect                        # update MEMORY.md item by item and write today's diary entry
bin/reflect --light                # update MEMORY.md from the day so far, no diary
bin/tick --detach                  # what cron runs: start the beat in the background (log: state/tick/beat.log)
bin/mentions                       # read mentions into the inbox
bin/mail                           # read mail into the inbox
bin/doctor                         # is this checkout safe to boot? (--live: is the spine healthy?)
bin/proofs --text                  # how far each countable DIRECTIVE.md proof has got (read-only)
bin/proofs --ladder --text         # the autonomy ladder: each capability's level, and what the next one needs
```
